summary: Sell the equal-weight S&P 500 fund: it ended Thursday below its 50-day average, the line I set for selling it, so I keep that promise; the health care fund is still above its line and stays, and the cash waits for a clear buy-back signal or 10 December at the latest.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Thursday 19 November it was worth $966.94 against $942.17 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund. The lead grew to about $25 on Thursday. Most of that came from yesterday's sale: the S&P 500 fund SPY was sold at the open for about $737 a share and ended the day at $715.87, so selling saved about 2.9% on that money. Seven trading days is still far too short to call this skill.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Thursday opened higher, as futures had suggested, and then reversed. The S&P 500 fell about 2.0%, the Nasdaq about 2.3% and the Dow about 2.2%, more than 1,100 points. That was a sixth straight down day for the S&P 500. The worries were the same as all week: whether heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, with the newly listed Anthropic shares falling back from their first-day highs, and a Federal Reserve that is expected to raise interest rates again.
- Almost every part of the market fell. All eleven sector funds I watch were down, from about 0.7% for energy to about 2.8% for consumer companies. The bond funds were the only ones that rose, by less than 0.2%.
- UnitedHealth fell another 5.5%. The health care fund XLV fell 2.05%.
- This morning, before the open, futures point to the S&P 500 about 0.3% to 0.7% lower and the Nasdaq 100 about 1% to 1.5% lower. Intuit is down about 10% before the open despite better results than expected. Traders now put the chance of a Fed rate increase on 9 December near 99%. The 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.0% to 5.05%. Tension around the Strait of Hormuz continues, with a ship reported struck by an unknown object off Oman. The final November consumer sentiment survey comes out at 10:00 a.m. New York time, after the open.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. RSP: sell all of it. When I bought it I wrote that it would be sold if it ended a day below its 50-day average, and yesterday I wrote that the next decision would sell it if that happened. It ended Thursday at $211.63, below its 50-day average of $214.95. The line was broken, so I sell. Its earlier advantage over SPY has also narrowed: over five days RSP fell 4.1% against 5.5% for SPY, a much smaller gap than before. With SPY already sold, the proceeds stay in cash, as I wrote yesterday.

2. XLV: keep. It ended Thursday at $177.46. The line I set yesterday was a close below $176, or a widening of the Medicare proposal to cut payments for drug makers or hospitals. Neither has happened: the price is about 0.8% above $176 and 0.7% above its 50-day average of $176.26, and I found no new change to the Medicare proposal beyond the insurer share prices falling further. It is down about 7% from what I paid, close to the 8% loss limit (about $175), so it sits right next to two lines that would both send it out. I would not buy more at this price. If it ends any day below $176, the next decision sells it.

3. Cash. After the sale the account will hold about $826 in cash, about 85%. That is a large bet against a fully invested benchmark, and I want to be plain about it. It is the result of rules written before the fall, not a new view that the market will keep falling. The reason still holds: the broad market is below its long-run trend, the Fed is about to raise rates with near certainty, and long-term interest rates are above 5%. The end date stays as written: the account goes back to being fully invested no later than the first trading day after the Fed decision of 9 December, that is 10 December. The buy-back signal comes first if it arrives: SPY ending two trading days in a row at least 1% above its 200-day average, about $740 today, which is 3.4% above Thursday's close. I looked again at a Treasury bill fund (SGOV) for the cash: for a stay of under three weeks the interest, about 0.25%, is close to the cost of buying and selling it, so it stays as plain cash. Longer bond funds are not a safe place either, because they lose value if the Fed's increase pushes long-term rates higher. Gold (GLD) is still falling hard, down about 20% in 60 days.

I also asked whether the account should buy something new instead of holding this much cash. Every sector fund fell on Thursday, and buying into a falling market to reduce the cash would be a guess, not a reason. The plan says positions need a specific, checkable reason; I do not have one today.

This is not the first decision of the month, so there is no monthly review. The first is due at the start of December.
risks: The biggest risk is that the account is now about 85% cash, close to the opposite of the benchmark. If the market rebounds sharply, which is common after six straight down days, the account will fall behind quickly and will only buy back once SPY ends two days at least 1% above its 200-day average, which could be well above today's price. Selling RSP after a fall may lock in a loss just before a bounce. XLV is within about 1% of its sell line, so it may be sold soon too, leaving the account almost entirely in cash. Prices before the open can change by 9:30, and the consumer sentiment figures and Fed speeches today were not out when this was written. Several facts about Thursday and this morning come from a single news summary, and its figures for the 10-year yield differ slightly between articles.

orders.reason: Ended 19 November at $211.63, below its 50-day average of $214.95, the line set for selling it when it was bought.
